Towards Robust Long-Lived Agents: Benchmarking Experience Lifecycles in Evolving Environments

Shijue Huang ††thanks: Equal contribution. Affiliation: The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology    Hangyu Guo11footnotemark: 1 Affiliation: The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology    Hengheng Zhang Affiliation: Huawei Inc.  ReScopeBench.github.io     github.com/JoeYing1019/ReScopeBench    Guo An Affiliation: Huawei Inc.  ReScopeBench.github.io     github.com/JoeYing1019/ReScopeBench    Zhitao He Affiliation: The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology    Qi Tian   Yiren Feng22footnotemark: 2 ††thanks: Corresponding authors. Affiliation: The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology Affiliation: Guangdong Laboratory of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Economy (SZ) Affiliation: Huawei Inc.  ReScopeBench.github.io     github.com/JoeYing1019/ReScopeBench
Abstract

As agents become more capable, they are moving beyond one-off tasks toward sustained assistance across successive user goals. Such assistance requires agents to discover how unfamiliar environments work, reuse what they learn across tasks, and keep that experience current as environments evolve. Existing benchmarks increasingly study experience reuse and adaptation, but provide limited insight into which parts of accumulated experience agents revise, retain, or lose. To address this gap, we introduce ReScopeBench, a benchmark for the experience lifecycle across 18 interactive environments. It distinguishes structural experience about how an environment is organized and accessed from rule experience about reusable principles and constraints that guide decisions across tasks. To study how experience is acquired, reused, and revised, we propose an experience-first construction approach. It builds task streams around shared experience and introduces silent environmental changes. We evaluate task performance and track changes in saved experience throughout each stream. Across 20 models, we find that retained experience improves task performance, but agents struggle to keep it current as environments change. Even when the required experience is correctly recorded, agents do not always fulfill requests successfully. These findings identify selective maintenance and effective use as complementary challenges for long-lived agents.

1 Introduction

Recent advances have strengthened agents’ ability to complete complex tasks in interactive environments (OpenAI, 2026; Anthropic, 2026; Seed, 2025b; Gonzalez-Pumariega et al., 2026; Lin et al., 2026). This progress opens the way to sustained assistance across successive user goals. In an initially unfamiliar environment, such assistance requires the agent to discover how resources are organized and which rules guide its actions. When new requests depend on the same resources and rules, agents can reuse earlier discoveries to guide their work. Continued reuse also requires keeping this experience current when the environment changes.

To evaluate these abilities, existing benchmarks examine experience reuse across tasks and adaptation to change. Memory benchmarks test retrieval and reasoning over supplied histories, with some also assessing information updates (Maharana et al., 2024; Wu et al., 2025; Tan et al., 2025; Hu et al., 2025). Interactive and skill-oriented benchmarks assess experience acquired through agents’ own actions and reused or refined in later tasks (Zheng et al., 2025; He et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026; Lei et al., 2026). AgingBench and EvoArena further examine memory maintenance and adaptation as information and operating conditions change (Zhu et al., 2026; Xu et al., 2026).

However, existing evaluations do not fully show whether agents update outdated experience while keeping the parts that remain valid after the same environmental change. Task success alone cannot answer this question. For example, a delivery directory may move while its delivery policy stays the same. An agent may find the new directory and complete the task but leave the old path in memory. It may also rewrite the saved entry and lose policy details that are still valid. These cases can receive the same task score as an update that corrects the path and keeps the policy. When queries and task actions share a limited budget, repeated lookups leave fewer resources for completing requests. We therefore evaluate task results together with the experience agents save. We track what agents learn, update, retain, or lose across tasks and environmental changes. Table 1 compares existing benchmarks and ReScopeBench along these dimensions.

To support this evaluation, we introduce ReScopeBench, a benchmark spanning 18 initially unfamiliar environments. We focus on two complementary types of experience that agents can acquire in these environments. Structural experience describes how resources are organized, related, and accessed. Rule experience captures reusable principles and constraints that guide decisions across tasks within an environment. To study how the same experience is acquired, reused, and revised, we propose an experience-first construction approach. We first identify structural and rule experience that agents can discover through interaction, then build varied tasks in which agents can reuse it. Local changes invalidate selected parts of this experience while leaving others valid. Changes are unannounced, so agents must detect them through interaction. To examine experience maintenance at different stages of interaction and beyond a single change, we vary change positions and include multiple changes in some streams. Without exploration costs, agents could repeatedly rediscover information instead of maintaining useful experience. We therefore place discovery and execution under environment-specific resource budgets, encouraging agents to reuse valid experience and selectively recheck what may have changed. We evaluate task performance with and without retained experience and assess saved content against private references that reflect the current environment.

We evaluate 20 commercial and compact open-weight models on ReScopeBench and find that retaining experience improves average task performance. Agents generally record structural experience more completely than rule experience. When environments change, they preserve much of the valid content but leave some outdated content uncorrected. More interaction after change does not always coincide with more explicit attempts to update saved experience. Even when the required experience is correctly recorded, agents can still fail to fulfill requests. These findings highlight the need to update experience without losing valid content and to use saved experience effectively to complete tasks.

Our contributions can be summarized as follows:

  • •

    We introduce ReScopeBench to study the experience lifecycle in evolving environments. It evaluates task performance together with the acquisition, retention, and revision of saved structural and rule experience.

  • •

    We construct 352 tasks across 18 interactive environments, organized into streams in which agents can discover and reuse structural and rule experience. The streams include 26 controlled environmental changes that make selected experience outdated while other experience remains valid.

  • •

    Our evaluation of 20 models combines task outcomes, saved experience, and action traces. It reveals gaps in experience acquisition, incomplete revision of outdated content, and failures to fulfill requests even when the required experience is correctly recorded.

2 ReScopeBench

2.1 Benchmark Overview

ReScopeBench evaluates agents over task streams in initially unfamiliar interactive environments. We use ee to denote one environment, TeT_{e} its stream length, and t=1,…,Tet=1,\ldots,T_{e} the task position within that stream. For each task, agents receive a goal and descriptions of the available tools. They use these tools to discover resource relationships and operating rules, and can record these findings for reuse in later tasks.

Completing varied goals requires agents to locate relevant resources and understand how to act on them. We distinguish structural experience, which describes how resources are organized, related, and accessed, from rule experience, which captures reusable principles and constraints that guide decisions across tasks. For example, locating stored goods does not establish how they must be handled. Their location can change while handling rules remain valid, or vice versa. Separating these types lets us track their acquisition, revision after change, and retention of still-valid content.

To track how the same experience is acquired, reused, and revised across tasks, we propose an experience-first construction approach. We first identify discoverable experience, then build varied tasks that reuse it and local changes that invalidate selected parts. Changes vary in timing and number and must be detected through interaction without explicit notice. Resource budgets limit exhaustive rediscovery, encouraging agents to reuse earlier findings. Figure 1 summarizes the construction process and lifecycle. We evaluate task performance with and without retained experience and assess saved content against references for the current environment.

2.2 Benchmark Construction

As depicted in Figure 1(a), construction proceeds through environment preparation, experience discovery, joint stream synthesis, and verification.

Environment Preparation.

We implement each environment ee as a simulated application in code, using application scenarios and public documentation to define its entities, workflows, and operations. Each simulation provides reproducible initial states and tools whose outputs reflect the current state. Tool descriptions explain how to use the interfaces, while local resource relationships and operating conditions must be discovered through interaction. Each environment specifies which tool operations incur costs and the limits on the resources they consume.

Experience Discovery.

The selected experience must support multiple task goals and be discoverable through the tools available to evaluated agents. We identify candidate experience by inspecting environment code and data, then verify its discoverability through tool interactions. For each selected item, we record its scope, the observations that reveal it, and the decisions and task outcomes that depend on it. These links form a private dependency graph for constructing tasks that reuse the experience and changes that invalidate selected parts.

To assess the saved content, we organize the selected experience within each environment ee into reference units uu. Each unit groups related statements, called claims cc, about resource relationships or operating rules. Each claim has a scoring rubric specifying what the saved content must establish to count as correct. The references reflect the environment version at each task and remain private to the evaluator. Appendix D.1 illustrates a rubric and its application.

Joint Stream Synthesis.

To test reuse across different goals, we use the dependency graph to construct an ordered stream of TeT_{e} tasks for environment ee. The tasks share resource relationships and operating rules but vary in their requested objects and conditions. To test selective revision, we schedule local changes immediately before selected tasks. Their positions form the change schedule 𝒟e\mathcal{D}_{e}, with each d∈𝒟ed\in\mathcal{D}_{e} denoting the first task affected by a change. Each change alters selected relationships or rules and updates their reference claims. For a given change and affected unit uu, let NuN_{u} denote the current-version claims describing information introduced or changed by that event. Later tasks use both changed and unchanged information. Changes are detectable through tool observations but are not announced in task instructions or boundary messages.

We complete the tasks in sequence using the tools available to agents, carrying state forward and applying scheduled changes. These tool-call sequences serve as private reference solutions. We use the resulting task artifacts and relevant final states to specify each task’s delivery requirements. A private grader checks the agent’s delivered results against these requirements and accepts equivalent valid outcomes. Appendix D.1 gives an example. We then compare the resource costs of reference solutions, local correction after changes, and exhaustive searches over candidate resources and rules. Budgets cover verified completion and correction costs while restricting exhaustive rediscovery.

Verification.

Starting from each environment’s initial state, we replay the reference solutions in task order and apply the scheduled changes. We check that each solution produces the required outputs within budget and that the grader assigns the expected score. We also test tool-call sequences that reveal updated information and support local correction within budget. Finally, we inspect task instructions and tool interfaces for leaked answers and unintended shortcuts. We freeze the tasks, tools, budgets, change schedules, and graders before evaluating models’ ability to acquire, reuse, and revise experience.

2.3 Benchmark Statistics

ReScopeBench contains 352 tasks across 18 environments and nine application domains. Each environment exposes 3–18 tools (10.1 on average). Task streams have 16, 24, or 32 tasks and contain one to three environmental changes. The 26 changes occur at different positions, with the first change between tasks 5 and 13. Figure 2 groups these events by change type and environment domain.

We distinguish six mechanisms by what changes in the environment. Rule changes alter the conditions governing valid actions and outcomes. Structure changes alter resource locations, identifiers, or relationships. Permission changes alter which actors are authorized to perform an operation. Resource changes alter the availability of items, capacity, or time slots. Tool-path changes alter which existing tools or tool sequences can complete an operation. Mixed changes combine two or more mechanisms within the same event. These categories describe environmental changes, whereas structural and rule experience describe what agents learn. Appendix A provides the environment inventory and change schedules.

2.4 Evaluation Protocol and Metrics

2.4.1 Evaluation Protocol

For each model–environment pair, two streams start from the same initial state with identical tasks, tools, budgets, and change schedules. Agents are instructed to store structural experience in memory and rule experience in skills. The with-experience condition retains these assets and retrievable history across tasks. The without-experience condition clears them between tasks. Both conditions permit within-task learning and start each task with a fresh conversation. Environment state persists within each stream and can diverge as agents take different actions.

2.4.2 Metrics

We report three performance metrics for task outcomes and four experience metrics for the coverage, updating, and recovery of saved experience, each scored from 0 to 100 with higher values indicating better results. The experience metrics use post-task memory and skill snapshots from the with-experience stream. Appendix B.2 details aggregation.

Task performance.

To assess whether retained experience helps agents complete tasks and how they perform when a change first affects a task, we report baseline performance (BP), experience-enabled performance (EP), and drift-onset performance (DP). For a fixed model, let se,t+s^{+}_{e,t} and se,t−s^{-}_{e,t} denote task scores with and without experience in environment ee at task tt. We use the stream length TeT_{e} and change schedule 𝒟e\mathcal{D}_{e} from construction to define

BPe=1Te​∑t=1Tese,t−,EPe=1Te​∑t=1Tese,t+,DPe=1|𝒟e|​∑d∈𝒟ese,d+.\mathrm{BP}_{e}=\frac{1}{T_{e}}\sum_{t=1}^{T_{e}}s^{-}_{e,t},\quad\mathrm{EP}_{e}=\frac{1}{T_{e}}\sum_{t=1}^{T_{e}}s^{+}_{e,t},\quad\mathrm{DP}_{e}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}_{e}|}\sum_{d\in\mathcal{D}_{e}}s^{+}_{e,d}. (1)

DP measures performance after executing the first affected task, including adaptation during that task.

Experience coverage.

Task success does not show how much experience an agent has correctly saved for later tasks. We therefore use structural coverage (SC) and rule coverage (RC) to measure how much of the corresponding current-version reference inventories is correctly recorded. An LLM judge 𝒥\mathcal{J} receives the entire saved memory and skill corpus together with one reference experience unit. It assesses the unit’s claims against their rubrics, regardless of where the content is stored. Each claim scores 1 only if all required and applicable checks pass, and 0 otherwise. SC and RC average claim scores within units, units within each type, and all task positions, then multiply by 100.

Experience updating.

After a change, agents need to record the required updates while keeping experience that remains valid. We use update coverage (UC) to measure the fraction of update targets correctly recorded after the first affected task, and recovery timeliness (RT) to measure how early all update targets and previously correct, still-valid claims are recorded correctly together. For a fixed model and a change at position dd in environment ee, consider each affected unit uu and its update targets NuN_{u} defined during construction. Let VuV_{u} contain the current-version counterparts of its still-valid claims credited after task d−1d-1. The nonempty set NuN_{u} is shared across models. Both sets remain fixed over an LL-task window beginning with the first affected task and ending before the next change or at stream completion. Within this window, local position k=1,…,Lk=1,\ldots,L corresponds to stream task t=d+k−1t=d+k-1. Let zc,kz_{c,k} indicate whether claim cc is correct after that task. We define

UCu=100|Nu|​∑c∈Nuzc,1,RTu={100​(L−τu+1)/L,τu​ exists,0,otherwise.\mathrm{UC}_{u}=\frac{100}{|N_{u}|}\sum_{c\in N_{u}}z_{c,1},\qquad\mathrm{RT}_{u}=\begin{cases}100(L-\tau_{u}+1)/L,&\tau_{u}\text{ exists},\\ 0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases} (2)

where τu=min{k:∀c∈Nu∪Vu,zc,k=1}\tau_{u}=\min\{k:\forall c\in N_{u}\cup V_{u},\ z_{c,k}=1\} is the first task at which all required claims are correct together. RT records this first completion, not whether correctness persists at later checkpoints. Because update targets do not depend on prior mastery, both metrics can include first acquisition as well as revision.

3 Experiments

3.1 Experimental Setup

We evaluate 20 models from ten families: three compact open-weight models (Qwen3.5-9B, Qwen3.5-35B-A3B, and Qwen3.8-27B) (Team, 2025b) and 17 models offered through commercial services, including models with public weights. The commercial group covers GPT (OpenAI, 2026), Claude (Anthropic, 2026), DeepSeek (DeepSeek-AI, 2026), Doubao (Seed, 2025a), Gemini (Team, 2025a), GLM (GLM, 2026), Kimi (Team, 2026), MiMo (Xiaomi, 2026), MiniMax (Lai et al., 2026), and Qwen3.8-Max. These reports describe the model families. Table 2 lists the versions we evaluated.

All models use the Hermes agent harness (Nous Research, 2026) on the same 18 environments. Each model completes one with-experience stream and one without-experience stream per environment, following the protocol in Section 2.4. Task outcomes are scored by deterministic graders. We use GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI, 2026) to assess saved experience against the reference rubrics. Appendix B provides inference settings, runtime limits, and detailed execution and scoring procedures.

3.2 Main Results

Table 2 reports the main results. We highlight three observations.

(1) One compact model approaches the commercial median in immediate updating. Qwen3.8-27B records 29.05% of the required updates after the first affected task, close to the commercial median of 29.75%. Its task performance with experience shows a wider gap (62.48 versus 73.44). Both Qwen3.5 models score below 3 on each of these metrics.

(2) Rule coverage remains uneven even among strong models. Structural coverage exceeds rule coverage for 17 of 20 models, with a mean gap of 4.79 points. This imbalance is not confined to models with low coverage. GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol have structural scores above 70, yet their rule scores trail by 9.51 and 10.97 points, respectively. Claude Opus 5.5 reverses this pattern: its rule coverage of 73.22 leads the table and exceeds its structural coverage of 71.70. Strong structural coverage therefore does not uniformly translate into equally complete recording of rules, and the balance between the two types remains model dependent.

(3) High recovery scores can coexist with limited immediate updating. No model exceeds 37.63 in UC, leaving substantial gaps in recorded updates after the first affected task. Model rankings also differ between immediate updating and recovery timeliness. GPT-6 Astra ranks second in RT but tenth in UC, whereas Gemini-3.8-Flash ranks second in UC but ninth in RT. Strong recovery over subsequent tasks should therefore not be taken as evidence of a prompt initial response to change.

3.3 Analysis

We examine how experience relates to task performance, how models adapt to environmental change, and how their tool use and experience maintenance respond.

3.3.1 How Do Experience and Task Performance Evolve Across Tasks?

To examine how experience relates to task performance, we track paired task scores and post-task structural and rule coverage across all 20 models and 18 environments. We group environments by stream length (16, 24, or 32 tasks), keeping the same environments equally weighted at every position.

Gains accumulate across tasks. The upper row of Figure 3 shows rising performance with experience across all three groups, while performance without experience remains low. In the 24- and 32-task groups, shared change onsets interrupt these gains, followed by recovery. The 16-task group combines different change positions, so its average has no single common disruption.

Coverage losses differ by experience type. Coverage is scored against the current reference, so it can fall when previously correct content becomes outdated. In the 24-task group, performance drops at both T09 and T17. Structural coverage falls by 18.92 points at T09 while rule coverage stays comparatively stable. At T17, rule coverage falls by 15.97 points while structural coverage changes little. The two coverage measures distinguish mismatches that task scores alone cannot identify. Appendix C.1.1 gives the individual environment curves.

Coverage and performance can diverge. GPT-5.4 gains structural coverage across all three groups, yet its overall task performance remains far below the other displayed models. Coverage spans the full reference inventory, whereas successful delivery requires the relevant knowledge for a particular request and its effective use. Overall coverage therefore cannot substitute for task performance. Appendices C.1.3 and C.1.2 provide correlation and request-level analyses.

3.3.2 How Do Models Adapt Across Different Change Contexts?

We examine performance recovery and selective experience revision under different change timings, counts, and mechanisms. Performance comparisons cover all 20 models, 18 environments, and 26 changes. Performance advantage denotes the task score with experience minus that without experience. In event-aligned comparisons, offset zero is the first affected task, and +3+3 is the fourth.

Later events have higher average scores. Figure 4(a) shows no consistent increase in the first-four-task performance advantage when comparing single-change environments by onset position. The lower curves compare full task-score trajectories by change count. In two-change streams, mean with-experience scores over the first four affected tasks rise from 55.94 after the first event to 62.15 after the second. The corresponding means in three-change streams are 68.62, 70.50, and 72.53. Later events therefore coincide with higher average scores, although different tasks and change content prevent interpreting this as faster recovery.

Similar drops, different recovery. In Figure 4(b), the resource group has the largest immediate loss of performance advantage, at 40.33 points. Structural and tool groups show similar losses of 35.98 and 36.63 points from the task immediately before change to the first affected task. By the fourth affected task, however, the structural group is only 0.16 points below its pre-change advantage, while the tool group remains 8.69 points below. Initial disruption thus does not capture the remaining loss after several tasks. These are descriptive comparisons across different environment groups.

Revision remains incomplete. Figure 4(c) follows 487 cases across eight environments, each combining a model, reference experience unit, and change event to distinguish revision failure from missing prior knowledge. Each case correctly records all relations selected for updating and at least one still-valid relation before change. Over the first four affected tasks, replacement-content coverage rises from 21.47% to 64.63%, while still-valid coverage remains between 88.07% and 91.07%. Revision thus remains less complete than retention within this previously learned subset. The trajectories also reflect when tasks expose replacement evidence. Bands span the interquartile range of model means. Appendices C.2.1 and C.2.2 examine this exposure and subsequent persistence.

3.3.3 How Do Agents Allocate Tool Use?

We analyze 7,040 with-experience tasks across all 20 models and 18 environments to examine interaction allocation and responses to change. History tools retrieve prior records, experience tools read or modify memory and skills, and environment tools query or act on the current state. We count explicit calls, including failures, and exclude background review. Changes are aligned at the first affected task. Appendix C.3.1 gives the counting and averaging procedures.

Models differ in history retrieval. In Figure 5(a), the four displayed models make similar numbers of environment calls, ranging from 13.07 to 13.81 per task. History calls vary much more, from 0.14 for GPT-5.4 to 6.41 for GPT-5.5. Their differences in total activity therefore largely reflect consultation of prior records, rather than more requests to the current environment.

Interaction peaks near change. A tool round comprises one assistant turn with one or more calls and their responses. In Figure 5(b), the overall mean rises from 10.72 rounds over the three preceding tasks to 12.70 at onset, then falls to 11.21 by the fourth affected task. All displayed models except GPT-5.4 show a similar increase near change, indicating that the aggregate response is not shared uniformly across models.

Interaction and writing can diverge. Figure 5(c) compares write attempts over the three preceding tasks with the first affected task. Although GPT-5.5 uses more rounds at onset, its write attempts fall from 1.08 to 0.97 per task. GPT-6.1 Sol increases from 1.31 to 1.94, and GPT-6 Astra from 0.89 to 1.23. More interaction therefore need not coincide with more attempts to modify saved experience. These counts measure writing activity, not correct revision, which Figure 4(c) assesses separately.

4 Related Work

4.1 Experience-Based Agent Adaptation

Experience-based adaptation methods differ in what they retain from interaction and how they update it. Reflexion and ExpeL turn feedback and trajectories into verbal reflections or reusable insights (Shinn et al., 2023; Zhao et al., 2024). Other methods retain procedures: Voyager stores executable skills (Wang et al., 2024), while Agent Workflow Memory abstracts recurring action sequences into reusable workflows (Wang et al., 2025). To keep guidance current, Dynamic Cheatsheet revises test-time memory as new evidence arrives (Suzgun et al., 2026). ReScopeBench complements these methods with an evaluation of how acquired experience is reused and maintained across tasks as local conditions change.

4.2 Benchmarking Agent Memory and Experience

Benchmarks study experience under supplied histories, interactive tasks, and changing conditions. LoCoMo, LongMemEval, and MemBench evaluate reasoning over supplied histories, with the latter two also assessing updates to remembered information (Maharana et al., 2024; Wu et al., 2025; Tan et al., 2025). MemoryAgentBench adds incremental learning and selective forgetting (Hu et al., 2025). Interactive benchmarks, including LifelongAgentBench and MemoryArena, evaluate experience use across tasks (Zheng et al., 2025; He et al., 2026), while skill-oriented benchmarks study acquisition, refinement, and transfer (Zhang et al., 2026; Lei et al., 2026; Gao et al., 2026). More recent benchmarks examine maintenance as information and environments change. AgingBench (Zhu et al., 2026) studies memory degradation and revision, including agent-managed workspace scenarios. EvoArena (Xu et al., 2026) evaluates evolving terminal workflows, codebases, and preferences, and measures whether saved memory contains evidence of user preferences. In ReScopeBench, tasks reuse discoverable structural and rule experience, and local changes make selected parts outdated. We assess saved content alongside task outcomes to distinguish correction of affected relationships from retention of those that remain valid.

5 Conclusion

This paper introduced ReScopeBench, a benchmark for studying experience acquisition, reuse, and revision across 18 interactive environments. Its experience-first construction builds varied tasks around shared structural and rule experience, then introduces silent changes that invalidate selected content while leaving other content valid. Evaluations of 20 models show that retaining experience improves task performance, but rule experience is generally recorded less completely than structural experience. Further analyses show that agents preserve much of the still-valid content while leaving required updates incomplete, and can fail to complete requests even when the required experience is correctly recorded. More interaction after change does not always coincide with more explicit attempts to update saved experience. ReScopeBench offers a testbed for developing agents that selectively revise outdated experience and effectively apply what they retain.

Appendix A Benchmark Environments and Changes

This appendix expands the environment inventory in Section 2.3. Table 3 lists task goals, stream lengths, and tool counts for all 18 environments. Counts exclude the eight shared experience and history tools. Table  lists all 26 scheduled changes in the evaluated versions. Each change position denotes the first affected task.

A.1 Task Goals and Tools

A.2 Complete Change Catalog

The catalog uses the six change mechanisms defined in Section 2.3. We classify events by their effect on environment operations, rather than the names of modified fields. For example, Cinema’s replacement pricing plans revise rules, whereas Railway’s replacement train services change available resources.

Appendix B Evaluation Details

B.1 Experimental Setup

We evaluate the 20 models in Table 2 on the same 18 versioned environments. Each model completes 352 tasks per condition, covering 26 environmental changes. We use the maximum supported reasoning effort where configurable. Explicit sampling settings use temperature 1 and top-pp 0.95; unsupported or omitted fields follow provider defaults. Foreground execution allows 100 agent iterations per task and up to 65,536 output tokens per response. An iteration may contain multiple tool calls. Environment-specific resource budgets apply separately.

The Hermes memory and skill interfaces are pinned to revision 345cd2b057a45. Memory and skills are limited to 16,000 and 100,000 characters, respectively. Agents receive a memory snapshot and skill index at task start and can retrieve full skills on demand. Four read-only history tools retrieve completed-task records through lexical matching and pagination, with a shared limit of 30 calls per task. Structural and rule experience are classified by content, regardless of where they are stored. No reference experience is preloaded.

Both conditions start from the same environment state and use a fresh conversation for each task. With-experience streams retain memory, skills, and retrievable history. Without-experience streams clear these assets while retaining their own environment state. The two states then evolve independently through agent actions. Each model–environment pair has one stream per condition. GPT-5.5 also supported environment development. Agents can update experience during execution. Hermes skill review can run after ten tool iterations and a completed, uninterrupted response, with a separate limit of 100 iterations and 600,000 cumulative input tokens. It uses the same model, cannot access environment tools, and finishes before grading, so the current task’s score cannot supervise review. Later history retrieval may include permitted outcome feedback, but never private reference answers.

B.2 Scoring and Aggregation

BP and EP average all task positions, including the initial task. DP uses the first affected task after each change and includes adaptation within that task. SC and RC average binary claim scores within reference units, units within each experience type, and checkpoints within each environment. References follow the current environment version and include content not yet encountered by the agent.

GPT-6 Astra evaluates one complete reference unit against the complete saved memory and skill corpus per request, using medium reasoning effort and a 14,000-token output limit. Model-identifying metadata is withheld. Each claim receives credit only when all applicable rubric checks pass. Equivalent wording and supported deductions are accepted, while unresolved contradictions receive no credit. We validate the structured responses and cited evidence before computing scores. These metrics measure reference coverage rather than the precision of all saved content.

For each affected unit, UC measures coverage of the current update targets after the first affected task. RT measures the first checkpoint at which all update targets and the unit’s previously correct, still-valid claims are correct together. Update targets are shared across models, while the retained set depends on pre-change credit. Both target sets remain fixed within an LL-task window starting at the first affected task and ending before the next change or at stream completion. Only units with nonempty update targets participate. Completion at its first or last task scores 100 or 100/L100/L, respectively, and no completion scores zero. An empty retained set reduces the criterion to update completion. RT records first completion, not its subsequent persistence, and reflects the opportunities provided by the task schedule.

All metrics weight environments equally. DP averages events within environments. UC and RT average affected units within events, then events within environments. Avg. averages the seven unrounded metrics. Longer streams and larger inventories do not receive more weight.

Supplementary analyses use Wm​e​tW_{met} and Bm​e​tB_{met} for task scores with and without experience, and Sm​e​tS_{met} and Rm​e​tR_{met} for post-task structural and rule coverage. The difference Δm​e​t=Wm​e​t−Bm​e​t\Delta_{met}=W_{met}-B_{met} is distinct from DP. Position curves keep environment membership fixed within each stream-length group and equally average environments and models. Model interquartile ranges describe variation across models, not uncertainty across repeated runs. Inapplicable observations are excluded rather than scored as zero.

B.3 Cross-Judge Consistency

We rejudge all 7,040 checkpoints from 20 models and 18 environments with GPT-6.1 Sol, holding saved content, references, rubrics, prompts, and inference settings fixed. The second judge does not see the first judge’s decisions. The comparison covers 121,717 distinct unit-level requests and 433,850 claim decisions. All requests specify Sol without fallback. Of valid responses, 81.0% carry an explicit Sol deployment label and 19.0% an opaque provider identifier.

The judges agree on 98.79% of structural and 99.24% of rule claim decisions. Across 360 model–environment pairs, Pearson correlations for SC, RC, UC, and RT range from 0.9808 to 0.9985, as shown in Figure 6. The aggregate structural–rule coverage gap remains positive with both judges (4.79 points for Astra and 3.86 for Sol). Agreement is weaker in some environments, particularly SAP structural coverage. These results support consistency under the shared rubric, rather than independent validation of judgment accuracy.

Appendix C Supplementary Analyses

This section provides additional evidence for the three analyses in Section 3.3: experience and task performance, adaptation to environmental change, and action allocation. Complete-stream analyses cover all 20 models and 18 environments. Request-level analyses use Filesystem and Oracle, where verified mappings connect required experience, saved content, and observable actions.

C.1 Experience and Task Performance

C.1.1 Complete Per-Environment Trajectories

Figures 7 and 8 show the environment-level variation behind the aggregate trends. They plot complete task streams, with markers for GPT-5.4, GPT-5.5, GPT-6.1 Sol, and GPT-6 Astra as in Figure 3. Dark-gray curves equally average the same 20 models at every position. The first figure shows task performance in both conditions. The second shows post-task structural and rule coverage in the with-experience condition, measured against the current reference. Vertical lines immediately precede each change’s first affected task.

C.1.2 Task-Required Content and Request Outcomes

To relate saved experience to delivery, we align each request’s required structural and rule bindings with saved claims, submitted arguments, and delivered artifacts. Figure 12(a) summarizes the first-submission paths. The trace cohort covers 640 with-experience tasks, 2,560 requests, and 8,826 foreground tool calls with matching responses across all 20 models in Filesystem and Oracle. We select these environments for their verified mappings, rather than as a random sample.

A request at task tt has complete prior experience when every required structural and rule claim is credited at checkpoint t−1t-1 under the same reference version. Credit requires all required and applicable rubric checks to pass. Prior experience is incomplete if any mapped claim lacks credit. The 320 requests on initial and change-onset tasks have no same-version predecessor, so their prior status is unknown. The remaining 2,240 requests comprise 1,014 complete-prior and 1,226 incomplete-prior requests.

We compare complete and incomplete priors within each model’s tasks that contain both groups and have resolved submission attribution. This yields 326 model/environment/task cells, 1,304 requests (625 complete-prior and 679 incomplete-prior), and 36 model/environment cells across 18 models, without selecting on delivery. We compute each group’s rate within a task, then average over eligible tasks, models within each environment, and the two environments equally. Both groups share task cells and outer weights. Eligible tasks vary across models: 5–14 in Filesystem and 5–10 in Oracle.

Figure 9 shows higher delivery with complete prior experience in all 36 model/environment cells. Complete- and incomplete-prior delivery rates average 94.74/69.16% in Filesystem and 95.88/73.40% in Oracle. The cross-environment rates are 95.31% and 71.28%, a 24.03-point gap. Requests without a linked submission account for 19.42 points, submissions that never become compatible for 4.58, and compatible submissions without delivery for 0.03. The gap therefore mainly concerns whether requests reach submission.

Table 5 separates four mutually exclusive outcomes. Compatibility requires all frozen structural and rule bindings, while delivery is assessed from the resulting task artifact. An incompatible submission can be corrected before delivery. This decomposition is descriptive: matched requests can still differ in targets, ordering, remaining budget, and within-task discovery. In raw counts, 21 complete-prior requests fail delivery and 458 incomplete-prior requests succeed. Complete saved prior experience is thus neither necessary nor sufficient for delivery in this cohort.

C.1.3 Lagged Experience–Performance Associations

We next examine whether prior coverage remains associated with performance after accounting for model and task variation. We pair checkpoint t−1t-1 with task tt only within the same reference version. Excluding 360 initial and 520 change-onset observations leaves 6,160 observations at 308 environment/task positions. Unlike the request-specific prerequisites above, these predictors cover the full reference inventory.

Across model means, structural and rule coverage correlate strongly with with-experience performance (Pearson r=0.956/0.975r=0.956/0.975), but also with baseline performance (0.898/0.9280.898/0.928). The coverage measures correlate at 0.9650.965. We rank models within each task, average tied ranks, and adjust coverage and with-experience performance for contemporaneous baseline performance within each environment. We compute partial rank correlations per environment and average them equally. Figure 10 then adds model/environment and environment/task fixed effects, followed by model/environment-specific linear position trends, using the same observations.

The structural/rule associations fall from 0.436/0.4470.436/0.447 after baseline adjustment to 0.187/0.1400.187/0.140 with fixed effects and 0.149/0.0960.149/0.096 with position trends. The fully adjusted raw-score counterparts are 0.137/0.1240.137/0.124. Much of the aggregate association thus overlaps with differences among models, tasks, and stream progression. These descriptive adjustments do not identify a causal effect of saved experience. Residualizing either WW or W−BW-B on BB yields the same residual, so the two adjusted results provide the same evidence.

C.1.4 Acquisition and Loss of Previously Credited Content

We distinguish claims never credited from claims credited earlier but not currently, using all 20 models in the 15 environments unchanged through T08. The cohort and reference version remain fixed. At T04, the structural–rule coverage gap is 4.06 points: never-credited content contributes 4.725 points, while lost credit contributes −0.662-0.662. By T08, the gap narrows to 2.18 points. The early rule shortfall therefore mainly concerns content not yet correctly recorded, rather than loss of previously credited content. This decomposition does not equate the difficulty or evidence exposure of structural and rule claims.

C.2 Environmental Change and Experience Maintenance

C.2.1 Selective Revision of Previously Correct Experience

To distinguish revision from first acquisition, we track relations credited immediately before a change. A model/unit/event case is eligible when every changed target has a credited one-to-one predecessor for the same semantic relation and at least one unchanged target is credited. The preserved set contains only these previously credited unchanged targets and remains fixed. This yields 487 cases across 20 models, eight environments, and 11 events.

For a changed or preserved target set AA, coverage at post-event offset kk is

CA,k=100​∑a∈Awa​ca,k∑a∈Awa,C_{A,k}=100\frac{\sum_{a\in A}w_{a}c_{a,k}}{\sum_{a\in A}w_{a}}, (3)

where ca,kc_{a,k} is current-target credit and waw_{a} is the reviewed lineage weight, normalized within the target set. We average units within events, events within model/environment pairs, eligible environments within models, and models equally. Membership and weights remain fixed across the four offsets. Case eligibility can differ across models because it depends on prior acquisition. Many-to-many replacements and partitioned targets, including Railway pool replacements and Cloud partitioning, lack one-to-one predecessors and are excluded, not scored as failures.

Updated-content coverage rises from 21.47% to 43.07%, 59.40%, and 64.63% over the first four affected tasks. Preserved-content coverage is 89.05%, 88.07%, 90.38%, and 91.07%. At the fourth task, preservation exceeds updating in 19 of 20 model means and all eight environment means. Revision thus lags retention in this cohort. These trajectories follow the actual task schedule, and changed and preserved targets can differ in complexity and when they become relevant or observable.

To examine revision after replacement evidence becomes visible, we inspect the Filesystem subset: 122 changed model–relation pairs in 70 eligible model/unit/event cases across 20 models. We match each replacement binding to a successful list_delivery_lanes response by workspace, lane, and destination, then check its existing post-task claim score. Exposure accumulates within T07–T10 before each checkpoint. Table 6 partitions this fixed cohort using raw counts, unlike the macro-averaged coverage above. “No mapped read” does not exclude evidence from other channels, such as history or successful writes.

Of the 118 pairs exposed by T10, 104 receive credit at the checkpoint of their first matched read. Yet 26 exposed pairs lack credit at T10: 12 have never received it, and 14 received it earlier but lost it. Saved records illustrate two failures. At T07, Qwen3.5-35B-A3B records new Ember lane identifiers in memory while retaining conflicting old identifiers in a skill. Qwen3.8-Max records and receives credit for the new identifiers at T08, but omits them at T10. Observing replacements therefore does not ensure that saved experience stays current and internally consistent.

C.2.2 Persistence after First Completion

RT records first completion but not persistence. We therefore follow all 2,340 affected model/unit/event observations, including those outside the prior-correct cohort. Completion requires simultaneous credit for all current update targets NN and the fixed unchanged targets VV credited before the event. With empty VV, it measures update completion only. We track each first completion over two further checkpoints within the same reference epoch.

Of 1,632 observations that complete at least once, 1,520 have both follow-ups. Among them, 1,364 remain complete at both checkpoints and 156 (10.26%) become incomplete at one or both. Another 112 completions lack sufficient follow-up, and 708 observations never complete. Figure 11(a) shows all four outcomes. The 10.26% regression rate uses only the 1,520 eligible completions. First completion thus does not guarantee completeness over the next two tasks. Regression here means lost credit, not necessarily permanent forgetting or impaired task performance.

C.3 Interaction and Action Allocation

C.3.1 Tool Use Across Environments

Figure 5 uses 151,569 foreground tool calls from all 7,040 with-experience tasks. Tool interfaces determine the categories. Environment tools query or act on the current environment. History tools retrieve prior episodes and records. Experience tools access or modify saved memory and skills. We count explicit requests, including failures, and exclude automatic memory loading and background review. A tool round is an assistant turn containing one or more calls with matching returns. Write counts include recognized requests to create, modify, or delete experience. An unidentified operation remains in the experience-call total but not the write count. One write can affect multiple entries, and the number of writes does not measure the amount or correctness of revised content.

For Figure 5(a), we average tasks within each environment and then weight the 18 environments equally, retaining zero-call tasks. Panels (b) and (c) use all 26 changes with the same observations at every offset from −3-3 to +3+3. We average events within environments before averaging environments. The overall mean then equally weights all 20 models. In panel (c), Before averages offsets −3-3 to −1-1, and At change denotes the first affected task at offset zero. Task requirements vary across positions, so these comparisons describe observed behavior rather than isolate a causal effect of change. An unchanged write count does not rule out different written content, later writes, or updates during background review.

C.3.2 Request-Level Action Paths

To examine the actions behind request outcomes, we use the Filesystem and Oracle trace cohort described in Appendix C.1.2. Its 8,826 foreground calls comprise 2,189 environment actions, 2,160 environment queries, 1,813 experience operations, and 2,664 history queries. Counts include failures but exclude automatic memory injection and background review.

First-submission paths use only evidence visible before the assistant turn that generates the arguments. A parallel read in that turn cannot inform them. We classify requests by first-submission compatibility and whether a successful response for their scope preceded submission, retaining no-submission and unknown categories. The matched cohort has no unknown cases. Figure 12(a) merges the two incompatible-submission paths. A response within a request’s scope need not resolve every required binding. Compatible first submissions before successful feedback about the request account for 85.14% of complete-prior requests and 7.92% of incomplete-prior requests. This association appears before such feedback could guide a correction, although the recorded sequence does not identify which information source the agent used.

Read categories describe returned evidence, not intent. A first-observed singleton supplies one accepted current binding with no earlier singleton or candidate-set exposure through the instrumented interfaces and no same-version prior credit. A prior-credited query returns a binding credited at checkpoint t−1t-1. A re-observed singleton repeats an earlier visible binding when prior credit is absent or unavailable. The latter two categories are re-queries. Candidate sets include the accepted value among alternatives, while mixed responses contain multiple statuses. Failed and unmatched reads remain separate. Earlier evidence carries across a change only if its type, unit, condition, field, and complete accepted-value set are unchanged.

Figure 11(b) counts each environment query once: 42.6% are first-observed singletons and 21.2% are re-queries.

The trajectories in Figure 12(b) and (c) average calls per task across all 20 models, including tasks with no reads. Across complete pre-change and post-change epochs, first-observed singletons fall from 2.53 to 1.14 per task in Filesystem and from 1.86 to 0.15 in Oracle. The epochs are T01–T06 versus T07–T16 in Filesystem and T01–T10 versus T11–T16 in Oracle. Re-queries rise from 0.39 to 1.08 and from 0.47 to 0.84, respectively. These means weight tasks equally, unlike pooled call proportions, and do not isolate the effect of change.

In the matched 1,304-request cohort across 18 models, 201 requests receive no linked submission: 133 in Filesystem and 68 in Oracle. We inspect terminal resource receipts and states to check whether omissions coincide with exhausted budgets. Filesystem capacity is the smaller of the remaining write attempts and remaining calls to environment tools. Oracle capacity is the shared balance divided by the two-unit correction cost, rounded down. All 133 Filesystem omissions retain capacity for a write attempt per omitted request. In Oracle, 61 of 68 omissions leave insufficient budget for even one correction. This contrast also holds with complete prior bindings: all 10 Filesystem omissions retain write capacity, while all six Oracle omissions do not. The eight Filesystem tasks containing those 10 omissions end normally below the model-turn limit.

These balances describe terminal resources, not availability at decision time or delivery under alternative actions. Appendix D.2 illustrates the trade-off between checking and execution at Oracle T10. Call counts exclude tokens, latency, and background work. Domain-specific resource units are not pooled.

Appendix D Illustrative Case Studies

D.1 Local Revision and Subsequent Reuse

Figure 13 follows GPT-5.5’s Riverlight Ledger binding after a silent destination change before T07. At T09, the agent rechecks public evidence and updates the directory handle while preserving five valid executable fields. The revised binding supports five later deliveries (T11–T14 and T16) without further environment queries for the manifest.

The case also contrasts the two scoring procedures. The experience claim specifies the directory for Grove’s amber lane. Applying the reference rubric to saved content, the LLM judge scores it 0 at T07 and 1 at T09. The programmatic task grader instead checks the delivered artifact and final state. Its five checks award the selected T09 request 25/25 points, while the full task scores 75/100.

D.2 Using Saved Experience under a Budget

Figure 14 illustrates the execution difficulty examined in Appendix C.1.2: complete saved experience may still yield incomplete delivery under a resource budget. At the start of Oracle Clinical One T10, all four models have recorded the required structural and rule bindings. Four corrections cost eight units, leaving room for one five-unit context read within the 17-unit budget. A second read makes full delivery unaffordable. GPT-5.4 spends 15 units on three reads and completes one correction. GPT-5.5 and Claude Opus 5.5 complete all four with eight units. Doubao-Seed-2.1-Pro does so after one read, using 13. GPT-5.4 and Doubao-Seed-2.1-Pro retain an inactivity warning about one requested record, providing context for checking. One targeted check remains compatible with full delivery, while further checks consume the budget needed for execution.
